utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I see, Mr. Ierace, you're on your feet. Is there anything you wanted to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will keep it brief. Yesterday afternoon, I met with Defence counsel and we discussed the proposal that the Prosecution call tomorrow a witness to give evidence in relation to the shooting and editing of videos and electronic photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I made the offer that the witness be made available to the Defence prior to him giving evidence. That offer was declined. The Defence expressed concern that they did not have a statement. Mr. President, I can inform the Trial Chamber that there is a statement, in part, as to what the evidence will be. The witness's name is Zoran Lesic, L-e-s-i-c. The statement has been disclosed to the Defence some time ago. The date of the statement is the 21st of November, 2001. The statement covers the shooting, that is, the taking of the video, and I would seek your leave, Mr. President, to ask the witness, during his evidence, questions going beyond what is in the statement, to include the taking of the photographs and the method by which they were joined. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, any observations as far as the -- or Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. What the Defence would like is not that it should be informed alone, but that everybody can be informed, and that we have, from an expert, statements which are quantifiable and can be verified and that we be kept abreast. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps a way around this dilemma is, since the issue has been raised by the Defence, that from this point on, until such time as the evidence is called, the videos and the 360-degree photographs not be tendered but rather be marked for identification, so that after the Defence has had the opportunity to hear from the witness, at that point the Prosecution would then formally seek to tender the remaining material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question for you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If the witness would be called -- it is mainly you that wanted to have more information, and I do understand that you also wanted quantifiable and verifiable, but would you have any questions to put to a witness who is able to explain whatever technical aspects there are as far as the shooting and the redacting of these photos and videos is concerned? I mean, I would like to avoid the situation where the witness has been called and where you would have no questions to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understood that so far the Defence seems to have had too many questions, and we would, of course, have questions for that witness too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's useful to call the witness. Then, Mr. Ierace, you may call the witness. As far as marking for identification or tendering into evidence is concerned, we should not forget that, I would say, the whole technical issue of admitting into evidence is a technique which is mainly used in, I would say, common-law environments, where it is of vital importance to keep a close eye on what will be presented to a jury and what will not be presented to a jury, while the law of evidence in a mixed, in a hybrid system, or in civil-law systems mainly is a matter of the evaluation of the evidence which is available; and exclusion of the evidence would mean, in a common-law environment, that you keep it away from those who will decide, while in a hybrid system it's, I would say, more a question of whether you take into consideration -- whether you allow to take into consideration any evidence that, although presented to you, should be excluded from your mind. Being in a mixed system at this moment, I do not see any specific reason why these videos should just be marked for identification, since it would not be for the first time that material that is admitted into evidence in this Tribunal would later be excluded, or at least the admissibility would be reviewed and then perhaps the material would be declared not admissible into evidence. Since a matter of evaluation, it's still open even when some portions of the evidence might have been admitted. This wouldn't mean that it, therefore, under all circumstances will be taken into consideration by the Chamber. Having explained this, so you may call Mr. Lesic. And you intend to do that tomorrow morning, as far as I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We could do it at any stage tomorrow. It's at the convenience of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. In view of the fact that my colleagues and I had a meeting yesterday, I should like to get information from my colleagues with respect to the order of witnesses to be heard today and tomorrow, because we were saying that there would be witnesses tomorrow for incident number 6. But I didn't receive any information yesterday as to whether those witnesses will, indeed, be present tomorrow. So I should like to ask my learned colleagues and the Trial Chamber, as far as possible, to adhere to the witness list for witness testimony that we received because we very often seem to have alterations. And I was told yesterday afternoon that we are going to have two witnesses tomorrow which are not on the list and schedule for tomorrow. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do recall that yesterday you indicated that there might be some problems as far as the travelling of witnesses was concerned. If there's any further information, would you please give it to the Chamber and also so that the Defence is informed. Apart from that, if there are changes on the order of calling the witnesses, of course it's of vital importance that the Defence is informed as soon as possible. And if you would have any specific problems with a certain witness, please let us know, Ms. Pilipovic, indicating exactly when you received information about the change of the order of calling the witnesses. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can give that update now. Indeed, I gave it to my friends yesterday afternoon. I'm surprised to hear what has just been said. The next witness will be Mensur Jusic, followed by Witness M, followed by Witness H, followed by Zematica, Faheda Zematica. I said as much to my friends yesterday, and of course we will fit into that schedule Zoran Lesic. The two witnesses about whose arrival became unsure yesterday were Witness H and Zematica. But it became clear during the meeting with the Defence yesterday that those problems were resolved, and I said as much to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. One of the advantages of the schedule I gave to you is that you can just take out all witnesses that have been already heard and just keep the order or change the order. And I now see that on the 4th of February, we received Mensur Jusic part of the schedule, and on the 5th of February, a Ramiz Grabovac. And of course, if you don't put them in order, I don't know who will be first, who will be next. So one -- I would suggest that whenever you issue a new schedule, that you indicate whether there are any changes in respect of the order earlier given to the Defence, and that you list all those witnesses not yet examined in the order you intend to call them so to have a better view on what will happen. Because schedules with just one name on it, I especially intended to always have an overview of what will happen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to thank the Chamber for its understanding. I should just like to inform the Chamber that yesterday afternoon, we were told that Witness H and Zematica would be heard today or tomorrow. I think that is a very short time, but we are prepared to cross-examine those witnesses, although it was short notice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear - although I do understand your difficulties, that you are nevertheless ready to cross-examine the witness. I think, then, we are at the point where Mrs. Taric could be brought into the courtroom in order to be cross-examined by -- would it be you, Ms. Pilipovic, or Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Taric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I do understand that you can hear me and you do understand me. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, you'll now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for having come to this courtroom. To begin with, I would like to refer to what you said during your testimony yesterday. Is it correct, madam, that your place of residence was what we generally call the Heros' Square?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, madam, in the square, or near Heros' Square, was there a building that was commonly known as Loris, the Loris building?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you spoke about your family. You're married; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the brevity of your answer. Could you tell us the profession of your husband; what does your husband do?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband works in MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, could you tell us, please, what MUP stands for?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a crime inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, and what education and training has your husband had?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An inspector school, school for inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, throughout the period of the war, that is, from May 1992 until the end of 1995, what were the duties and functions of your husband?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I object here, please, because we're not talking about my husband; we're talking about myself and my child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects to this line of questioning on grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please indicate the relevance of your questioning at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be happy to, Mr. President. This witness and the answers she gave a moment ago has given two or more written statements. In her own written statements that I'm going to show to her, the witness said that her husband was a military commander. Now, I think that it is very important for us to learn certain things because this witness is linked to someone in her family -- that is, somebody in her family was a high military commander.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this point, Mrs. Taric, we're still at the point where the Court has to decide whether these questions can be put to you, so you don't have to answer them at this moment. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, our objection remains the same. First of all, Mr. Piletta-Zanin hasn't put to the witness what her husband was doing during the course of the war, number one. And number two, and perhaps more importantly, what would be the relevance of what her husband was doing during the course of the war given that this witness has testified about an event involving herself and her daughter outside of their home, walking down the streets of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin and Mr. Mundis, the mere fact that the witness has until now testified about an incident would, as such, not exclude any specific reason for that incident to happen. So the Defence should be in a position to establish whatever reasons there might have been for this incident. And it was not just accidentally that this incident happens. On the other hand, then we are in an area, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, where the Defence should indicate to the witness what its case is. So if you think that there's any relationship between the occupation of the witness of the -- of the husband of the witness and the incident, then you'd please explain to the witness what your case in this respect would be, and then, of course, you're allowed to establish whatever relationship, unknown to the Chamber at this moment, might have been there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, I'll put my question in a different way. You said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. yesterday -- we weren't able to see the photos very well. They were rather dark. But you did say that the incident took place close to the front lines; is that right? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near -- it did not happen near the front line. The demarcation line, as the crow flies, was about one kilometre away, so the confrontation line was a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when you're quoting, it's, of course, not the witness that should deny if there was any misquoting. If so, please, would you give the source of where the witness said that the incident took place close to the confrontation line, and perhaps also specify what you think of being close. Is that one kilometre, is that ten kilometres, is it fifty metres? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You spoke about the front line; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Madam, could you tell the Trial Chamber, which likes precision, at what distance the front lines were from the incident that took place.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just said that I'm not quite sure. I can't be precise. But as the crow flies, in a straight line, it would be about one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you spoke about the front line. Do you know whether the front lines corresponded to the trenches and trench lines?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you were, at the time, married to a man who was - and is it correct if I say that he was a military commander? And I would be happy to show you your statement, a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, did you give a written statement, I think in Sarajevo, on the 12th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Taric, if I can help you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin is referring to a statement which you would have given in 1995. He has the text in front of him and would like to ask, I think, some questions about your statement at that time and go, perhaps, through a few elements. So the first question is whether you gave a statement in 1995 to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you nevertheless signed the statement which was in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Who authenticated or verified that translation?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lady who was the coordinator there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should now like to submit to the partisan, the witness, the witness's statement in English. It was translated, and it is dated the 12th of November, 1995. It is number ERN 00360800, for the first page, and 01 for the second page, and it is a document provided us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You want to give it to the witness in order to verify her signature or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the statement to the witness to see whether it is indeed her signature. That is my first point. And also, my second point -- the document is a three-page document. The third page is 802; the last digits are 802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's our procedure that since the exact number is known, that it's not tendered into evidence and it's also not marked for identification, as we usually did. So would you first please give it and just -- Mrs. Taric, could you just verify on the pages in front of you: Is this your signature under it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then, please, return the papers to the usher. Mr. Usher, would you please give the original back to Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You know that if you want to confront the witness with part of the statement, that you read, literally, that part, and then put whatever questions you have on these parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to use the Serbian text so that the witness could read the text herself, and I think that everybody will be satisfied that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you would agree? Since this is the translation prepared by the Prosecution, I think it diminishes the risk of any misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the 12 November 1995 statement of the witness in the Bosnian language is not signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do know, but if it will be read in English, then it has to be translated anyhow to the witness, because you can't confront her with it in the English language. So I would think twice translating creates a greater risk of mistakes than just relying on the original text. If there would be any reason on the specific point to check whether the translation is correct or not correct, it could be done easily, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree? So then you may read it in the original language. Would you have for the interpreter's booth copies of the statement on this -- so that it will be -- yes, I see. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have a sufficient number of copies, but since I was already envisaging the objection of Mr. Mundis -- I was not envisaging this, so that I did not prepare too many copies of this. Can the usher please help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the interpreters' booth have copies. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see some of them having -- waving with papers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have the statement, Your Honour, in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in English. So I think -- no, they're not -- I see -- it's difficult for me because the glass is rather dark. Part of the interpreters have no copy - would you please provide them - and the others have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the B/C/S booth has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters, we shall be reading -- or rather, we shall be showing the passage on page 2, somewhere halfway down the page, and it starts: "I never saw or heard ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then please read it to the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think I'd rather have the witness read it, because it is in Serbian, and it will be better that she reads it in her own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you want to confront the witness with it, I would prefer you to read it to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I shall be happy to say it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said the following, in the language which is yours, and I will now quote you: "I never saw or heard that anybody was hit in that street. We were the first and the last to be hit from a sniper weapon on that street. I know that because my husband is a military commander and he knows the details." Now, I did not follow the interpretation at the same time, but, madam, did you hear what I said and did you understand what I read out to you?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, can we then agree that, as you said in your language, which I have just read, that your husband was a military commander?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I do not speak English, whether the interpretation is correct that my -- that it is the same thing for my husband to be a member in the -- a worker -- an employee of the MUP as a military commander when I was giving this statement that I was explained that that was one and the same thing, and when I signed it [as interpreted]. But I wanted to object on this occasion, that I'm here as a civilian victim and to leave my private life alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Taric, the Defence has the opportunity to put whatever questions that might be relevant. And the matter whether you are a civilian or not, of course, you testified on the incident that happened to you. But the Defence is entitled to see whether there are any backgrounds that they think relevant, so I would invite you to answer the question. And perhaps I'll help you to the extent that the question was, on page -- it's written in the English language, which you do not understand, but of which the English version was signed by you, that your husband was a military commander. The first question was whether you said this, of course not in English but in your own language, or that you did not say this to the investigators in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's an employee in the MUP, Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you used these wordings in 1995 or that you used wordings that he was a military commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Member of the MUP, an employee of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you said in 1995, as I understand, or is that your explanation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An employee of the MUP, a member of the MUP, not a commander. If it was translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say in 1995, you used the words "MUP" and not "military commander."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you told us a moment ago -- because I think that this matter now becomes fundamental for the Defence, this translation. Now, you told us that you signed a document in English because they were in the presence of one or two interpreters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And this interpreter evidently spoke your language?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And it was the interpreter's mother tongue, I mean the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And the interpreter, therefore, read to you your non-signed version in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, I am sure that I did not pronounce it well, but what you understand by the words "vojni zapovjednik," am I wrong or am I rather right that that clearly means a military commander?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Chamber what these two words mean that three interpreters interpret here as a "military commander"?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand it because I don't understand the role of the person who does it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Taric, I have the feeling that you might think yourself as in a position where you would have to defend yourself against questions with which you might think that one way or the other might attack you. There's no question about it. You just can answer the questions. If, for example, you would have used these words but -- let's say, you think that's still what I intended to say or I meant to say, please answer these questions. There's no reason to be nervous about it. Whatever you tell us, just tell the Court -- just answer the questions. The only thing that's of importance is that you answer the questions now to the best of your recollection, both of what you said in 1995 and what your recollection is as of today. So it's not necessary to start any debate with Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If you just quietly answer his questions, everything's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember -- as far as I can remember, because that was a long time ago, perhaps I did not pay enough attention to the interpretation when the translation was read out to me so I did not correct it then. But I do not think that this is an accusation because I know that my husband had nothing to do with the army save that he did -- except that before the war, he did the same thing as he's doing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If we come to a matter of translations, we have very high-quality translator, so it's in the transcript what you did read to the witness. So the meaning of that linguistically may be verified easily. I have one additional question: Are there any tape recordings of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a general rule, no, Mr. President. I can inquire whether there were any tape recordings made of this specific interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I find it extremely doubtful but I will make that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether there is any source for verification available to us. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we should like to tender the two documents, which is, (a), the statement in English, and the non-signed version in the Serbian or Bosnian language, because there is this problem which seems to us of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. utmost importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, I will continue now with my questions. You said that your husband is still doing the same job, but what were exactly his duties during the war?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we got that, but the fact that he worked in the MUP does not say what were his duties. What were his duties during the war, will you please?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a criminal investigation inspector, the job that he's doing now and that he did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, you should know, I think, more specifically if, after your incident, a police report was drawn?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, does that now mean that you don't know or that no report was made?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reports were made under those circumstances, in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you absolutely sure?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no record was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your recollection, please, you said that during that time, there was -- there was light, there was fire, that the weather was nice over Sarajevo, that the sky was clear over Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now I believe we have to produce a document, but I'm afraid we thought that we would hear one of the general objections, and therefore I should say that this is a document which was supplied by the Prosecution and which was a daily report of the UNPROFOR. It is the document which made difficulties yesterday, but this is the document of a same nature. We received it from the Prosecution, and now we should like to -- this is a slightly technical problem, so I have to ask the Chamber to solve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This kind of report, to the extent that if there's any part of the testimony of the witness which would cover any of the information in this report, it could be relevant as to the assessment of the credibility of the witness. So please proceed. Mr. Mundis, you know what the position of the Chamber is, so I think that's the reason why you just sat down. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago, I asked you if you spoke English. Now, I want to ask you if you can read English a little?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I will read to you a document, a part of it, but I need the leave of the Chamber to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If my learned colleague could please provide us with the date or ERN number of the document or a copy of the document, that would be quite helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I just intended to tell Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The Chamber does read English, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was about to do it. But the Defence -- shall I give one copy for each one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters do not have the text. Could it be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give several pages of the document to the usher. It is two pages. And I wish to inform every person present here that it is the first page, a rather important document. The document was not copied in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the first page of the document be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be D36.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. And are there any copies left for the... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will just make sure we don't waste any time. First of all, we have a rather voluminous report in front of us, and the second page bearing the S1994/674, 654 page covers the rest of the day, the Friday. Sorry, page 635.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you see, on your right-hand side, the page of the final report, [In English] 780(92), et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we also have the second page, which I would like to be placed on the ELMO. Here we are. Perhaps from the -- if we can ask from the technical booth if we can go a little bit further. Can we zoom out a little so that we go to the item A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Here we are. The interpreters have the entire text. I would like them to read to the witness the first paragraph, beginning, "Combat and shelling activity." Here we are. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Piletta-Zanin. "Combat and shelling activity. A thick fog over Sarajevo quieted all shooting, according to the Bosnian Serb agency SRNA." Then, underlined, "3284/." "UNPROFOR reported that the situation remained quiet in the city and on Mount Igman. Source(s) Agence France Presse." That's what you wanted to read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The reason why I did not want to read it is because I did not want the witness to feel it as some kind of -- too much of a direct question coming from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, madam, could you tell us, if you remember, of the weather, what it was like on the day of the incident? I've asked you about the whole day, and you told me that it was a sunny day. And so I am now asking the question again that you've heard, that you heard that there was a weather -- an official weather report, what it said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This document -- there's no indication that this is any kind of official weather report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is part of the report of the committee of experts. The witness may be confronted with the content of this report. What the reliability of this report is, of course, still can be tested, Mr. Mundis, so just confronting the witness with this document doesn't say that what's in the document is, as such, reliable or true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my objection went more to the form of the question, in which Mr. Piletta-Zanin said: "And so I'm asking now the question that you've heard, that you heard that there was --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you have before you an official document which states that there was a thick fog and that this thick fog was covering Sarajevo. You told us that on the day of the incident, the whole day, it was sunny. Madam, do you confirm what you have just told us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please give the exact source of where the witness said that it was sunny during the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked that question in French, and this is one of the problems that has to be addressed. I said, "the whole day," and this was a couple of moments ago. And I would like to look for it, but I cannot check the English transcript and check the translation. I believe it is "the whole day." So I think we can check in the transcript. I'm absolutely certain that the French transcript, which we could perhaps have a look at, is actually saying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 66, line 2 - I have the note here - it says "sunny day," but it doesn't say "the whole day." I don't know, really, but maybe we can try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can immediately check, but I think you have to allow me to just open the file of yesterday, which is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember from yesterday, we're talking about balconies, or people were sitting outside, drinking coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm doing a search now on the word "sunny." Your question yesterday was: "Was the sun shining? Was it raining, was it cloudy or overcast? Do you recall?" The answer was: "It was a sunny September day." That was the exact wording, at least in the English transcript, of what the testimony was, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It's at, as far as I can see, page 3119, line 20. And the witness testified that it was 5.00 in the afternoon. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. That's what the testimony was as far as the sun shining that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So I will now ask the question again, but I would like to check on today's transcript, if you'll allow me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I believe that we can see the problems that come from the English transcript, in page 19, for instance, line 8. You can see that there is something missing in my question in English. The English transcript reads -- or rather, has certain things missing, and I said in French what should have been interpreted into Serbian correctly. I actually used "the whole day."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm sure that there will be an opportunity for you to check exactly, on page 19, line 8, whether there was any maltranslation or something left out. Of course, I don't remember that, and I am listening with one ear English, one ear French. But if this would be the solution of five minutes' searching for the word "sun" in the transcript, then you're totally justified to have done so; if it's not, we've wasted five minutes of time. Because the word "sun," apart, perhaps, from that specific occasion - of course, there may be a mistake - but the word "sun" has not been used by the witness, and so whatever you would have said on page 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If you please allow me. Whatever your question may have been at page 19, line 8, at that moment no answer has been given by the witness. So that means that, since there's no word "sun" or "sunny" in the transcript of today, and since yesterday there was no testimony that would indicate that it was sunny during the whole day, while the witness said the incident took place at 5.00 in the afternoon, that I really do not see how there is a solid basis for the question which took our attention already now for five or seven minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. But this is a general problem, and I can check from tomorrow the French transcript and then we'll see what steps we'll take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm always interested to see the results of checking things, and not -- I'm not that much interested in whatever, by whomever party it may be, that they intend to check a lot of things, but I'm glad to see the results of this activity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would ask you the question again. You said that on the day of the incident, it was a fine day; the weather was good?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, it was a fine day. I have something to say, objection. The report I can see on the ELMO is observation of Sarajevo from Igman, from Mount Igman. And the weather can differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see, Mrs. Taric, because the document says more. It's not just about Mount Igman. You have testified that, on the day of the incident, it was a sunny September day. Mr. Piletta-Zanin gives us a report of a committee of experts which says, about the weather, that there was a thick fog reported by some agencies. And the question is: Being confronted with information about fog on that day, would this mean that your answer would not have been correct as far as the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure -- I am certain that in the city of Sarajevo on that day, there was no fog. It was a fine day. It was a warm day. I'm certain of it because of what I was wearing on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Witness. You said a moment ago that, as far as you were concerned, there was no -- there were no reports following the incident.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, I believe that you said that in wartime, there were no such police reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such reports that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know, madam, if after such incidents, UNPROFOR was informed of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you lived in the Heros' Square.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if there was a military command post near where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If you say that it was not that close, could you tell us where this post was, since it seems that you knew where it was?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 500 to 800 metres from our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, do you know what was there, who was there?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to return to the question of your husband. You said that you knew about certain things about what you said in your statement, and you put that in relation to your husband's functions, his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. duties. We saw that his duties were not the ones that we read about in the statement. How could you know of some things about the trenches, for instance, if your husband did not have a military function, and if you say yourself you did not go close, you did not approach those lines? And when I say "lines," I mean lines; I do not mean trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I may have missed it, but I don't believe the witness has mentioned the word "trenches" during any of her testimony, either yesterday or today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About trenches?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's my recollection that the witness said she didn't know about trenches since she had not been at the place, and the question was in relation to where the front lines were. So trenches have been part of the cross-examination until now. So if there's anything in the prior statement about trenches, I deny the objection. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No, what I had -- I corrected it immediately in my question. What I said was trenches, but what I meant was front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So in your statement, madam, you said that you knew about some things, that is, front lines, because your husband in a certain post. How could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you referring to the previous statement or are you referring to the testimony given in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am referring to the statement that we read from a moment ago which is from November 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no part has been read about front lines. It's my recollection, but just from my memory, that you read a line where the witness at this time gave a statement that she knew that this was the only incident in that street, and she knew that because her husband was a military commander. That is what is in my recollection, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm going to rephrase my question. You're absolutely right, Mr. President, and I'm going to ask the question again in relation to the snipers. Because in this statement we were talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... has been about -- as far as I remember, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that -- I'm not absolutely convinced that I agree with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with your questions, and I'll have a look at the transcript in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, in the statement that you made, I believe that it was in November 1995, I think it was 15th November, you said that you knew about certain things in relation to sniping because your husband held a certain post. This is in the Serbian and English statement. And it is about him being a military commander. Now, inasmuch as you say that your husband was not a military commander, how could you know certain things, those that you mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was war in Sarajevo, but we had work obligations. Considering that I am a teacher, I had to go from one part of town to another part of town to work. And because of trying to keep safe during moving through the city, during movement through the city, I had to know of the locations. I had to know the locations that were known as dangerous and those spots where I had to literally run. This statement I gave is the one where I said that I knew of certain spots, certain locations. I did not say anything else in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement in two languages, in English and in Serbian, it says that you knew about certain details about various incidents, sniping incidents, because your husband held certain functions, and that these functions were possibly erroneously named as being that of a military commander. Now, how could you know these details if your husband was not a military commander?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was going to work and coming back from work, I heard about the cases that often happened, not only in the area where I lived but in the entire city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody would get killed, somebody would get wounded from sniping bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would first give an opportunity to Mr. Mundis to...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to check the transcript from yesterday, but I believe the witness in her testimony yesterday indicated that she gathered the information the following day while she was in the hospital. I would also raise an objection with respect to the form in which my learned colleague continues to put this quote from the witness's previous statement to her by paraphrasing rather than, again, relying on her document or the statement that she has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would just give me one second to read the transcript at this moment, because I was at the same time checking another part of the transcript. One moment, please. The objection is sustained. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the -- what the witness said -- and I'll read it to you. She said: "I never saw or heard if anybody was hit in that street. We were the first and the last to be hit from a sniper weapon..." I have to apologise. Not sniper, but sniper weapon was mentioned. So that's correct. So I repeat: "We were the first and the last to be hit from a sniper weapon on that street. I know that because my husband is a military commander, and he knows the details." In your question, it says -- it says that you knew about certain details about various incidents, sniping incidents, because your husband named as being that of a military commander, et cetera, et cetera. The witness testified that on the basis of the knowledge of her husband, she knew that she was the first and last to be hit by a sniper weapon on that street. That's the testimony; nothing more, nothing less. Would you please be precise, again. Apart from that, it takes a lot of time from your time of cross-examination. But if you are more precise, I mean when I can reread it, you can do it as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But I thought that this was a procedure to follow, but I will be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, how did it happen that your husband could know the details of the facts that you were the only ones, the first ones ever to have been hit if he was not a military commander?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband did not know about this. And the spot where my daughter and I were hit, wounded on that day, this was a safe line, safe area to walk in. And this was where we went, not just us but other citizens of Sarajevo. We walked there safely in this particular location. And I'm talking about this location, I'm not talking about the next 20 metres to the left or to the right, backwards or forwards. I'm talking about that particular location, that spot. We were the only ones hit there. I'm not talking about the location where there were other cases, 15 metres from there, 15 to the left, 15 to the right, or 50 to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. I am just going to quote you: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... now about this." [Interpretation] Did I understand correctly from quoting you now?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about any --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not about precision. Mr. President, I'm sorry to waste time, but this is about precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said on the 15th of November that your husband knew very well about the details because he held certain functions. Did you make this declaration?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you believe that his employment, his place of employment, is a function, then I suppose that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, madam, that was not my question. You said on the 15th of November that your husband knew about the details because of his function. I am just asking you whether you stated this on the 15th of November, and I'm going to ask you the question incessantly, if need be.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that, because of the nature of his work, he probably did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, madam, could you tell us now why, because of his work, he was able to know these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, I think if the full paragraph from which Mr. Piletta-Zanin has been quoting the witness's statement back to her, if that full paragraph were put to the witness, I believe that that may help avoid this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe this is going to be a waste of time, but if it's necessary, I'm going to read the whole page. But I was only working on the quotations that were said a moment ago and that you yourself had read, and I was hoping I would get some answers. The question was: How could her husband know certain things if she said that there was no relationship between the military and the police? So I believe that I have a right to some answers from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Taric, could you tell us whether the position of your husband would provide you with any information as to whether other people were shot by sniper weapons approximately at the location where the incident took place? So that is to say, what you did say about it in 1995, was that based to some extent on the knowledge of your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. May I remind you that you usually take six lines to explain why you don't want to waste time and then put a question of one line. If you would just, in quoting, be precise, without indicating that you are very precise at this moment, and why you are very precise, and why it is nevertheless a waste of time that you are precise. If you would just come to the point, leaving out any unnecessary additional remarks. If you would please do that. And you now may continue, and I may remind you that the cross-examination took five quarters of an hour until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no interpretation in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. We're very sorry, but one of our sets is obviously out of order. We have already drawn the attention of the technicians, of the engineers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have -- no, we have no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One of the headsets -- one of the interpretation sets is out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have a technical problem, we'll have the break a bit earlier. Mrs. Taric, we have a technical problem. We can't hear the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two. Three. Can you hear now, Your Honour? One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear that. It has been fixed, so we will continue for a couple of minutes. Would you then, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, resume after my little crusade, and put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was the witness who was speaking, but I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I believe you were just explaining to -- defining what the labour obligation means.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The labour obligation is work that you do if there is a war. Under very difficult conditions, we were trying to preserve some vital things, such as education, to keep them going so that the instruction could go on. As I am a teacher, my duty was to go and work at my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mentioned schools. Were there schools open and did the children go to them?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but instruction did not take place in school buildings; it took place at other, safer places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you spoke about front lines a moment ago. Do you know, to your knowledge, whether there were trenches along those front lines?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just consult with my colleague, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My very last question: Did you report your incident to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was -- after my daughter and I were wounded, we were extended help in the hospital. What kind of procedure they used, what kind of reporting procedure they used, I know nothing about that, but I and my daughter, after we left the hospital, were issued the so-called discharge document, which is the finding, the doctor's findings, and how to go about our further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. No other questions. Now the Prosecutor. Do you have any questions, any further questions to ask of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will have a couple of lines of questioning for re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to see whether we'll have the break now or not. Any additional questions by the colleagues, then? I think it will be better to have the break now. I might have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some additional questions as well, not knowing yet what your questions will be. We'll then adjourn until 11.00. Mrs. Taric, there will be a short questioning after the break. It will not be very long, presumably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Taric, Mr. Piletta-Zanin earlier read you part of your statement of November 12, 1995. I'm going to read you a full paragraph from that statement, and I'm going to ask you if you recall making that statement to the investigators on that date. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This is what it says in your witness statement dated 12 November, 1995: "I never saw or heard that anybody was hit in that street. We were the first and the last to be hit by a sniper in this street. I know that because my husband is a military commander, and he knows the details. I learned later when I was in the hospital that within one hour, five persons were hit by sniper fire in that area, but not in the street. These people were taken to the same hospital. This was also reported on television." Mrs. Taric, do you recall making that statement to the investigator on 12 November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Objection. The way in which the first sentence has been formulated, according to my statement, and the translation perhaps is not the proper one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: By that answer, I assume you're referring to the phrase in which it indicates, "my husband is a military commander...."

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention on the latter part of that paragraph, wherein you stated that you learned later while in the hospital that other persons were shot by sniper fire in that area. Do you remember saying that to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I met those people in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you met those people in the hospital, did you speak with them about the location where they were when they had been shot?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall speaking to them about the specific location where they were in relation to where you and your daughter were shot on that day?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how close to the location where you and your daughter were shot these other individuals were shot?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One lady, perhaps in the same direction, in front, she was hit some 50 metres away from us. The other two individuals were to the right of that lady. But from our spot, they were approximately -- within a radius of 50 metres, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you made reference to five other people. Do you recall where the remaining two people were, approximately, in relation to where you and your daughter were shot?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I know the neighbourhood, the area, I could know judging by what they said, but I wasn't on the spot. I wasn't there, so I can't tell you the exact location, the exact spot. But the woman who was hit, I do know almost exactly the spot because there was a building where it said "Nolit" and it was in front of that building, as she was going into her own hallway, into her own entrance. That's where she was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to a question that I put to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. President, this is at page 78, lines 7 through 9. Unfortunately, I don't have the paginated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But yesterday at 1.16, Mrs. Taric, you said: "After the incident, we found out that the bullet had come from the other side, from the top of the hill, and the street in question is Ozrenska Street."

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you testified, "we found out," do you recall from whom you found that out? How did you come to know that the bullet came from Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the bullet came on my left-hand side, those were the lines, up there in the hill. That's where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mrs. Taric. My question is more directed at how you found that out. How did you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From individual talks, talking to people when they came to visit us in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember if that information also came from the other individuals who you spoke with at the hospital that had been shot in the same location on the same day?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are of the same opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Taric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As some new points were quoted by the Prosecution, do we have the right to ask the witness one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's one question on an issue not touched upon by the Prosecution in its examination-in-chief, I would allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, that being the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have just answered a question concerning your admission to hospital, where you met a certain number of people who were equally wounded, and my question is the following: Do you know the names of the persons you met on that particular day at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mrs. Taric, I have a few questions as well to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before putting a question to you, Judge Nieto-Navia also has a question. And perhaps, Madam Registrar, could you please prepare for my questioning already map P3105. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You said that your husband was working at the MUP, M-U-P. What's that? What's the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: What does he do there?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a crime inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Before the war, during the war, and after the war?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From 1978, he's been doing that job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could, please, the Exhibit P3105 be put on the ELMO. Mrs. Taric, yesterday Mr. Mundis asked you whether the "X" in the middle of the yellow line that you've drawn indicates the location where you and your daughter were shot, and your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the map, the "X," is that a red "X" which is just above the name of a street which - I don't know whether I pronounce it well - is Ivana Krndelja?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow with me from that "X" to the right, approximately five, six centimetres, where it says "Miljacka." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you now - you're pointing at it. That's fine - go back with me again to the left, to the cross, the red cross -- the red "X," I have to say. Could you please change the --

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I follow the yellow line to the left from that "X," it seems to be in the river Miljacka, and the "X," the red "X," seems to be where a street crosses the river. On the photos and videos we've seen, I've seen two roads crossing, but I did not see a bridge or a river. Would you please explain to me whether the red "X" is actually put in the right position, and if so, what could explain that I see no river on the photographs or on the video. I'm just trying to clarify an issue which is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the map, there is -- from this street towards the river, there is just one narrow street. It is -- actually, the map is -- seems to show something there, but it is the Omladinsko Setaliste, or youth promenade, and then the River Miljacka. So that on the photograph itself, and on the videocassette, the Miljacka River is not that close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're saying the map is not quite correct and not detailed enough?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The map's a good one, but the Obala 27 Juli, the 27th of July Street, is a street which is located to the right of the Miljacka. When I moved leftwards from the "X," when I went left, Dolac Malta, I crossed the Miljacka at Cengic Vila and crossed over to the other bank, the opposite bank of the Miljacka River, and then moved along Vojvode Radomira Putnika Street. And in between the 27th of July Street and the Radomira Putnika Street is where the River Miljacka flows past. I hope I have been able to explain that properly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to read again your answer, but Mr. Piletta-Zanin is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I do apologise for interrupting. But one of the problems that we have with the photographs are to be able to visualise it all properly. I don't know if we could put it to the test now and to show the photograph again so that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm questioning the witness at this moment. Of course, you could have raised the same issue. But perhaps it's good that we again show you the 360-degrees photograph and that you indicate on that photograph where the river would be. That might take a second to... Yes, we have the -- oh, it's just on the screen. Could perhaps the 360-degrees photograph be turned slowly. And would you please say "stop" at the moment where you can identify the river or the street crossing the river.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. May I speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The river can't be seen because if from the spot I was standing you look down the street, straight down the street, straight on, straight ahead, the Miljacka, the River Miljacka, according to my assessment, here we have the first building, the second building, and then down there, that's where the Miljacka River would be. So that the photograph could not comprise the Miljacka River as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that you had crossed the river already when the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If we look at the map, my movement from Hrasno going down Brace Ribar Street, and it is the yellow line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrasno, Brace Ribar Street, the whole of that street is Brace Ribar Street, and then it continues on to Ivana Krndelja Street, which is the street I was wounded in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the Miljacka River is a little further off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were approaching the Miljacka River when the incident took place, or did you go towards the Miljacka River or were you moving away from it?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was moving in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when I crossed, I would have arrived in the same street and the same building to fetch the textbooks, the school books, had I gone on another few metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then crossing the river to collect the textbooks or...

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't cross the river. I didn't cross it. May we look at the map again, please, a few more minutes. Let's take another look at the map. Hrasno, Brace Ribar Street, and then I reached Ivana Krndelja Street. The river remained to my right, remained on my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just ask you: The Ivana Krndelja Street, is that -- I have to change to the transcript. Yes, I see that the yellow line on the map goes in the direction of what is indicated on the map as the Miljacka River. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then -- so if you are going in that street, you went in the direction of that river, of the river?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What direction? Because it looks as if you would go in the direction of the river when we follow the yellow line. You see, the yellow line goes up to the point where the red "X" is, which seems --

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "X'd" spot was the spot I was wounded. Now, the yellow line indicates the crossing over the Miljacka River. When I went to hospital, I crossed over the river to go to hospital. When I was taken to hospital, that's when I crossed the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you had not yet crossed the river when the incident took place. You're still on the Ivana Krndelja Street? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yes, I mean. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How far away were you, approximately, from the river at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Actually, the interpreter is not quite sure whether that was a "yes" or a "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your first answer. I said you were on the -- were you still on the Ivana Krndelja Street when the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were approaching the river, going into the direction of the river?

utterances.speaker: NAFA TARIC [Resumed]
